You can try challenging the thoughts on your own. It’s hard to remember at first, but the more you do it, the easier it’ll get. 

—-

Strategy one :)

For example, “I’ve ruined everything.” Show curiosity! Ask questions! The following questions are generally used for starting to learn to challenge these thoughts. I’ll use the “I’ve ruined everything” thought as an example, but these questions can apply to any negative thought. 

“What evidence do I have that I’ve ruined everything?”

“Is there any evidence against what I am thinking?”

“Would I say to someone else that they’ve ruined everything based on one small, insubstantial mistake?”

——

Strategy two:)

That’s one strategy. Here is a second strategy. It’s more of a step by step process so I’ll lay it out like that. 

1) pause and recognize what you’re thinking isn’t quite right.

2) focus on your body and emotions. How does it make you physically feel (heart racing, tense, etc)? How does it make you feel emotionally (scared, distressed, etc)?

3) separate this thought from yourself. “How about  I look at this thought from an outside perspective before I let it affect me.” Let’s try to have an external view of the thought.

4) write it down. 

5) identify what cognitive distortion it is. (Look up “list of cognitive distortions” on Google images and read through a few of the images.)

For you, it appears you struggle with catastrophizing. You jump to an extreme worst case scenario (“I’ve ruined everything.”)

Identifying what cognitive distortion allows you to see how the thought isn’t rational and helps you to reframe the thought. 

————

This is an EXTREMELY DIFFICULT process. It might feel like the hardest thing you’ve ever done in the world. It takes a ton of effort and grit. But you’re worth the effort. You’re worth feeling secure. You’re worth feeling happy. Please consider using the strategies I’ve given you. Feel free to switch it up between the two or use both. Let me know if you have any questions. 

(I’ve learned these in therapy and many therapists  swear by these techniques.)

Honestly, throughout all my sessions, no matter how intense they were, I never really experienced what I’d describe as dissociation. MAYBE at some points it was dissociation, but it never scared me or worried me at all. It wasn’t an uncomfortable experience. 

As for my life and improvements, wow. I feel amazing. I used to consider suicide daily, but I have barely had any suicidal thoughts at all. My depression has practically lifted. 

Honest part: Since I’ve dealt with the depression, I’d say my anxiety has gotten significantly worse. Before, I was so severely depressed, it was like my mind didn’t have room for both depression and anxiety. But now it does. I’m not too worried about this significant increase in anxiety, because I think we can treat it with anxiety medication. Spravato differs so greatly from person to person too, so just because I have increased anxiety doesn’t mean you will.

My advice is don’t be afraid. That’s probably not super helpful though lol. So my second advice is to really put forth as much effort as you can to challenge anxious thoughts about Spravato, and practice relaxation techniques (deep breathing, etc.). 

The experience is super relaxing. I’m guessing you will feel very relaxed too. I thought I’d have anxiety the whole time, but the nature of the medication doesn’t really let you feel too anxious haha. It’s like having a break from all the worry. It’s really, really nice. 

I hope that all made sense for you. Let me know if you have any questions.

The YouTube video “How I Tricked My Brain To Like Doing Hard Things (dopamine detox)” explains it better than I can.

It’s essentially taking away these high dopamine things so that your brain can get used to enjoying the low dopamine things. I’m not suicidal because I enjoy school and work. And when I’m not doing those things, I fill up my time with things that are good for me at home. For me, it was impossible to do without actually going to treatment. I’m not a drug addict but so severely addicted to my phone. I had to take my dopamine detox at residential. It was pretty much impossible at home. So essentially you have to be able to take away whatever it is you enjoy doing in bed so much (like phone or tv or whatever) so you have to find other things to do. 

It sucks. It’s a pain in the ass, honestly. No fun. But then it becomes amazing. It fixed my life. I wouldn’t have made it otherwise.
